newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: British foreign secretary to cut short HK visit.
newsitem.headline: British foreign secretary to cut short HK visit.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind will cut short his visit to Hong Kong to return to London early for a key parliamentary vote, a senior official said on Saturday.
Rifkind, in Singapore for a meeting of Asian and European foreign ministers, was originally scheduled to fly to Hong Kong on Saturday evening and return home on Tuesday.
But a senior British official told Reuters that Rifkind's trip had been moved forward slightly and shortened to enable him to make it back for the vote.

In Hong Kong, Rifkind is due to meet Governor Chris Patten and Tung Chee-hwa, the man selected by a pro-Beijing commitee to run the territory after Britain hands over control to China at midnight on June 30.

If he had kept to his original schedule, Rifkind would have missed an important parliamentary vote on Monday, called by the opposition Labour Party over Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's handling of the "mad cow" crisis.
Prime Minister John Major's beleaguered Conservative administration needs all available hands present for the vote, which should be close.

"The foreign secretary will be leaving Singapore earlier than planned and arriving in Hong Kong at 6.00 pm (1000 GMT) this evening so that we can bring forward...his programme in Hong Kong," the official said.
"He is planning to leave on Monday morning so that he can get back to London to vote.
"His meetings with the Governor and the chief executive designate and others will take place on Saturday evening and Sunday," he said.
The Conservatives have the same number of parliamentary seats as all opposition parties combined, although they have 51 seats more than second-place Labour.
If Labour were to win the vote, Hogg would be forced to resign and a vote of no-confidence in Major's government could be triggered. Major's position would then be precarious.
Labour is 15-20 points ahead in opinion polls and Major must hold a general election by May 22. He is believed to favour May 1 but might be forced to hold an earlier poll.
